title: Reading: Vocabulary in Context
summary: How to answer every vocabulary question without a dictionary: explain-in-your-own-words, context clues, prefixes and suffixes, synonyms, idioms and figurative language, with worked examples and 20 practice items.

blocks.text: Vocabulary questions appear on every text of the Reading paper, and they become more valuable as the texts get harder. In Text 4 one sentence to explain can be worth 3 marks. You cannot use a dictionary, so you need a **method** for working out meaning from the text itself. This page teaches that method, the six types of context clues, how words are built, idioms and figurative language, and gives you lots of worked examples and practice.
What vocabulary questions look like

rows: In paragraph 2, the writer says, 'given a weekly allowance'. Explain in your own words what 'allowance' means.
Give one synonym or a short explanation: money given regularly (e.g. by parents) to spend.
Explain in your own words what the phrase 'a hectic schedule' means.
Explain both ideas: hectic (very busy, rushed) + schedule (timetable/plan).
Explain in your own words what this sentence means.
Explain three ideas, usually three key words or parts of the sentence.
What does the phrase '...' mean? (A, B or C)
Choose the option that matches the meaning in context, often for figurative phrases.

blocks.title: How these questions are marked
items: **One mark = one idea.** For a 2-mark phrase the examiner looks for two ideas, usually one for each key word. Explaining only one gives 1 mark; explaining one part partly can also give 1.
**Synonyms and explanations are both accepted.** Many different correct words can score, so you do not need the 'perfect' word.
**Your English does not need to be perfect.** The examiner rewards the meaning you show.
**Repeating the word from the text does not show understanding**, so it does not score. 'Roofless means it has no roof' is fine, but 'roofless means roofless' is not.

blocks.text: The 5-step method for 'Explain in your own words'

items: **Count the marks.** That is the number of ideas you need.
**Split the phrase** into its meaning parts. Usually each important word (noun, adjective, verb) is one idea: 'a | breathtaking | view'.
**Read the sentence before and after.** These are your clues: examples, contrast words, causes, results.
**Find a simpler word or a short explanation for each part.** Check it fits the context.
**Write one clear sentence** that contains all the ideas, then **test it**: put your explanation in place of the phrase in the original sentence. Does the sentence still make sense?

blocks.text: **Worked example (3 marks).** Text: 'High on the hill, the old fort gazes down on a restless harbour.' Question: Explain in your own words what this sentence means.

rows: idea 1: the ancient castle / old military building
idea 2: looks at it from above; it stands higher and faces it
idea 3: a port that is always busy and moving
'a port which is always busy, full of moving boats'

blocks.text: **Full-mark answer:** The ancient castle stands high above and looks over a port that is always busy and full of movement. (3 ideas = 3 marks.)
The six types of context clues
When you meet an unknown word, the text around it often explains it. Learn to spot these six clue types.

rows: is, means, is called, that is, commas or dashes
'The town is famous for its souk, a traditional open-air market.'
or, in other words, also, similarly
'The trip was arduous, or in other words, really exhausting.'
such as, for example, like, including, a colon
'Pack your toiletries, such as toothpaste, soap and shampoo.'
toiletries = things for washing and cleaning yourself
but, however, although, unlike, whereas, instead of
'Karim is talkative, but his brother is taciturn and rarely speaks.'
taciturn = quiet and does not talk much
because, so, as a result, therefore, due to
'The road was impassable because of the flood, so the bus turned back.'
the whole sentence and the writer's feelings
'The children squealed with delight when they saw the clowns.'

blocks.title: Use what you already know
items: **Theme knowledge:** if the text is about charity, 'sponsor', 'donate' and 'raise funds' are likely; see the Themes and topics page.
**Grammar clues:** is the word a noun (after 'a/the'), a verb (after 'to' or a subject), or an adjective (before a noun)? This narrows the meaning.
**Positive or negative?** Even if you only know that a word is positive, you can usually choose the right MCQ option or write a sensible explanation.

blocks.text: How words are built: prefixes
A **prefix** is a group of letters at the start of a word that changes its meaning. Knowing 15 prefixes helps you understand hundreds of words.

rows: un-, in-, im-, il-, ir-, dis-
unforgettable, inaccurate, impossible, illegal, irregular, dishonest

blocks.text: How words are built: suffixes
A **suffix** comes at the end of a word. It often tells you the **word class** (noun, adjective, verb, adverb) and sometimes changes the meaning.
**Worked example (1 mark).** 'After the earthquake, a row of roofless houses stood by the river.' Explain 'roofless'. → roof + -less (without) = **without a roof / with no roof on top**.

**Worked example (1 mark).** 'The prices at the new café are surprisingly affordable.' Explain 'affordable'. → afford (have enough money for) + -able (can be) = **cheap enough for people to pay / not too expensive**.
Word families
Words from the same family share a root. If you know one, you can guess the others. Questions may use a different form from the one you learnt.
Synonyms: choosing the right one

A **synonym** is a word with the same or a similar meaning. But many words have several meanings, and only one fits the text. Always use the **substitution test**: put your synonym in the sentence and read it.

rows: 'The school has seen a sharp increase in student numbers.'
'The museum is a must for any visitor.'
'The new rule will affect the whole school.'

blocks.text: Phrases, idioms and figurative language
Text 4 (literary non-fiction) is full of descriptive and figurative language. You must explain what it **means**, not what the words say literally.

rows: 'The streets were as quiet as a library.'
'The city was an oven in August.'
'The wind howled through the empty streets.'
the wind made a loud, long, sad sound
a fixed phrase with a special meaning
'Learning to drive was a piece of cake.'
verb + small word with a new meaning
'The trip was called off because of the storm.'
'I have told you a million times.'

blocks.title: Do not explain figurative language literally
blocks.text: 'The city was an oven' does NOT mean there was an oven. Ask: what do the two things have in common? (An oven is very hot.) Then explain that shared quality in context: the city was extremely hot.
MCQ meaning questions (and a 'find a word' drill)

items: For **'find a word that means...'** (a useful practice drill rather than a usual exam question): check the part of speech. If the meaning is 'very old' (adjective), look for an adjective: ancient. Copy it exactly with correct spelling.

For **MCQ meaning questions**: one option is usually a literal meaning (the 'word-for-word' trap), one is the opposite or unrelated, and one is the meaning in context. Choose the one that fits the whole paragraph.
Substitute each option into the sentence. The right one keeps the meaning of the paragraph.

blocks.text: **Worked example (MCQ).** 'Years after the factory closed, its noise still echoes in the memories of the villagers.' What does 'still echoes in the memories' mean? A The factory is still noisy. B The villagers still remember the factory clearly. C The villagers cannot hear well. → **B**. A is the literal trap: the factory has closed. C is unrelated.
Weak, partial and full answers

rows: To create/think of a new way of cooking a dish (recipe) that nobody else has (unique).
A very difficult, exhausting walk up (a mountain/hill).
'The market hums with life from dawn' (3)
The market is full of activity/noise and people (hums with life) from very early in the morning / sunrise (from dawn).

blocks.text: How to answer without a dictionary: a checklist

items: Do not panic at one unknown word: you rarely need every word to answer.
Look at the word parts: prefix, root, suffix.
Read one sentence before and one sentence after.
Look for signal words: such as, but, because, in other words.
Decide: positive or negative? noun, verb or adjective?
Make a guess and test it by substitution.
Write the meaning simply. Simple words are safer than impressive ones.

blocks.text: Practice: 20 vocabulary questions
Cover the answers. For each question, count the marks, find the ideas, then check.

items.q: 'Volunteers at the clinic receive no payment.' Explain 'volunteers'. [1]
items.a: People who work/help without being paid (because they want to).

items.q: 'The festival attracts thousands of spectators every year.' Explain 'spectators'. [1]
items.a: People who watch (an event/show).

items.q: 'Our journey was arduous: twelve hours on a bumpy road with no air conditioning.' Explain 'arduous'. [1]
items.a: Very difficult and tiring. Clue: the example after the colon.

items.q: 'The beach was spotless; not a single plastic bottle could be seen.' Explain 'spotless'. [1]
items.a: Completely clean (spot = dirty mark + -less = without). Clue: the restatement after the semicolon.

items.q: 'Tickets are non-refundable.' Explain 'non-refundable'. [1]
items.a: You cannot get your money back (non- = not, refund = give money back, -able = can be).

items.q: Explain 'a hectic schedule'. [2]
items.a: A timetable/plan of activities (schedule) that is extremely busy and rushed (hectic).

items.q: 'The old souk is a maze of narrow alleys.' Explain 'a maze of narrow alleys'. [2]
items.a: A confusing network where it is easy to get lost (maze) of small, thin streets/paths (narrow alleys).

items.q: 'The coach was a tower of strength for the team.' Explain 'a tower of strength'. [2]
items.a: Someone who gives a lot of support (strength) and whom others can depend on, like something strong and solid (tower).

items.q: 'Staying up all night to revise is a false economy.' What does 'a false economy' mean? A a way to save money B something that seems to help but actually causes problems C a shop with fake products [1]
items.a: B. You think you are saving time, but tiredness makes your exam worse.

items.q: Find a word in this sentence that means 'very old': 'Near the ancient temple, children sold modern souvenirs.' [1]
items.a: ancient

items.q: 'Rents in the city centre have skyrocketed.' Explain 'skyrocketed'. [1]
items.a: Increased very quickly and by a large amount.

items.q: 'Although the hotel looked modest from outside, the rooms were luxurious.' Explain 'modest'. [1]
items.a: Simple / plain / not grand or impressive. Clue: contrast with 'luxurious' after 'although'.

items.q: 'The teacher's praise boosted my self-confidence.' Explain 'boosted my self-confidence'. [2]
items.a: Increased/raised (boosted) my belief in my own abilities (self-confidence).

items.q: 'Waves of tourists wash over the town every summer.' Explain this sentence. [3]
items.a: Very large numbers of visitors (waves of tourists) arrive and fill/flood (wash over) the town every summer (time). Three ideas: large numbers, they fill the town, every summer.

items.q: 'The village seemed frozen in time.' Explain 'frozen in time'. [2]
items.a: It has not changed at all (frozen) for many years, so it still looks as it did in the past (in time).

items.q: 'She bit off more than she could chew when she joined four clubs.' What does the idiom mean? [1]
items.a: She tried to do more than she was able to manage.

items.q: 'The plan was put on hold.' Explain 'put on hold'. [1]
items.a: Stopped/delayed for a period of time (to continue later).

items.q: 'The desert stretched out, vast and silent, beneath a merciless sun.' Explain 'a merciless sun'. [2]
items.a: Sunshine/heat (sun) that is extremely strong, harsh and never stops (merciless = showing no kindness or pity).

items.q: Which prefix means 'wrongly', and which suffix means 'without'? Give an example of each.
items.a: mis- (misunderstand) and -less (homeless).

items.q: 'The museum's interactive displays let visitors touch and try things.' Explain 'interactive'. [1]
items.a: Allowing people to take part / do things with it, not just look (inter- = between, act = do).

blocks.title: كيف تشرح كلمة أو عبارة بدون قاموس؟
items: عدد الدرجات = عدد الأفكار. عبارة عليها درجتان؟ اشرح الكلمتين المهمتين كل واحدة بمرادف.
اقرأ الجملة قبلها وبعدها: ابحث عن such as (أمثلة)، but و although (عكس المعنى)، because و so (سبب ونتيجة).
قسّم الكلمة: un- / dis- = نفي، re- = مرة أخرى، -less = بدون، -ful = مليء بـ.
لا تكرر الكلمة نفسها من النص في إجابتك؛ اكتب كلمة أبسط بنفس المعنى.
التشبيهات والتعبيرات الاصطلاحية لا تُشرح حرفيًا: اسأل نفسك ما الصفة المشتركة؟
